question: On login, does WooCommerce replace the guest session cart rather than merging it, and does woocommerce_cart_loaded_from_session fire where the Technical Design assumes?
expected: On login, Woo replaces the session cart with the persistent cart, or keeps the session cart and discards the saved one, depending on path. It does not merge. Section 7 row 1 calls this the most delicate logic in the storefront.
observed: WooCommerce 11.1.0. Guest session cart held product 39; the user had a saved persistent cart holding product 40. Cart before login: [39]. After becoming the user and reloading from session: [39]. Guest item present: yes. Saved item present: no. The hook the Technical Design builds the merge on, woocommerce_cart_loaded_from_session, is a real action in this version: yes. Exactly one cart survived: the guest one. Woo replaces rather than merges, so the merge in CART-13 to CART-18 is Mizzey work and section 7 row 1 is right to flag it. Whichever side is dropped is dropped silently, which is what makes this the delicate one.

question: Is the BR-005 price snapshot genuinely native to WooCommerce, with the price frozen onto the order line item at the point the Technical Design assumes?
expected: Order line items store the price charged. Section 6 classifies this as Native and calls it the highest risk business rule in the register, one the platform already guarantees.
observed: WooCommerce 11.1.0. Order 27 for 3 units at 100: order total 300.0, line total 300.0. Product price then raised to 250. Same order re-read: order total 300.0, line total 300.0. The price is frozen onto the order line at sale. BR-005 holds natively and section 6 is right to call it already solved. Note this is the price only: cost is a separate promise, tested in P-017.
notes: BR-005, ENT-08, AC-09. Section 6 row, not a section 7 gap row, which is why gap_rows is empty: the design claims this one is already solved.

question: Do WooCommerce coupons stack freely with no priority or stacking policy, as BR-004 and the Technical Design assume?
expected: Coupons combine freely. There is no priority and no stacking policy. Section 7 row 3.
observed: WooCommerce 11.1.0 coupon schema exposes 26 fields: id, code, amount, status, date_created, date_modified, date_expires, discount_type, description, usage_count, individual_use, product_ids, excluded_product_ids, usage_limit, usage_limit_per_user, limit_usage_to_x_items, free_shipping, product_categories, excluded_product_categories, exclude_sale_items, minimum_amount, maximum_amount, email_restrictions, used_by, virtual, meta_data. Priority or stacking fields: none. individual_use is the only exclusivity control: all or nothing, not a priority. Two percent coupons (10% and 20%) on a 100 item: apply calls returned true and true, cart holds [p003a, p003b], total discount 30.0. Both coupons applied together and the schema carries no priority or stacking field. The order of application is the order they were added, which is not a policy. BR-004 and PROMO-16/17 are Mizzey work, and the ENT-11 promotion rules table is justified.

question: Is WooCommerce order placement idempotent by default, such that a repeated payment provider callback is safely a no-operation without the extension the Technical Design proposes?
expected: Some protection exists, and gateway callback idempotency is the integrator's responsibility. Section 7 row 12.
observed: WooCommerce 11.1.0. Order 42, payment_complete called twice with the same transaction reference PROBE-TXN-0001. Status after the first call: processing, after the second: processing. Date paid after the first: 2026-09-09T09:59:36+00:00, after the second: 2026-09-09T09:59:36+00:00. Transaction id stored: PROBE-TXN-0001. Stock left from 10: 9. Order notes recorded: 3. The second call did not reduce stock again, so Woo carries a guard on the order side: _order_stock_reduced is set on the first pass and respected on the second. That is real protection against a repeated callback for the SAME order. What this does NOT establish, and PAY-05 still needs: Woo protects a repeated callback against one order. It does nothing about a customer submitting checkout twice and creating two separate orders, or about a gateway retrying against an order that was meanwhile cancelled. Both are integrator work, so section 7 row 12 is right that callback idempotency belongs to Mizzey, and this probe narrows what is left rather than clearing it.

question: Is corex-kit-woo inactive scaffolding only, gating nothing in the running store, as the Technical Design's section 4 describes?
expected: corex-kit-woo is four files, being a blueprint, a gate and a service provider, and its own documentation describes it as reserving the seam rather than being a store kit. It is milestone M9 on the CoreX roadmap and it is not started.
observed: corex-kit-woo holds 4 PHP file(s) totalling about 204 lines: corex-kit-woo.php, src\WooBlueprint.php, src\WooKitGate.php, src\WooServiceProvider.php. Active on this site: no. It registers no post type, taxonomy, shortcode, block or template override. It hooks: before_woocommerce_init. Its only hook declares HPOS compatibility, which is boilerplate, not behaviour. It reserves a seam and does nothing else, exactly as Technical Design section 4 says. The custom epic pricing that rests on CoreX contributing no commerce is sound.
notes: This probe bears on the platform seam itself, not on a contracted user story, so stories is empty. Source: Technical Design section 4, 'The one that matters: there is no CoreX commerce kit'.

question: Does the candidate translation plugin translate Woo product data, including variations and attributes?
expected: WordPress is single language and Woo provides nothing for multilingual product or content data. The design assumes a commercial translation plugin, at about 107 USD per year, will translate product data reliably where the free options do not. Section 7 row 17 and section 11.
observed: WPML 4.9.7 with WooCommerce Multilingual 5.5.7 and String Translation, on WooCommerce 11.1.0. Active languages: ar, en. Seeded an English variable product with a global attribute (pa_p006size, 2 terms) and 2 variations. WPML produced Arabic product 49. It is type variable, carries 2 variations, and the pair share translation group '18' holding languages [ar, en]. The attribute taxonomy has 4 row(s) registered in icl_translations as tax_pa_p006size, and the Arabic product carries 1 attribute(s): pa_p006size. Product, variations and attribute taxonomy all cross the language boundary and stay linked as one translation group. The design assumption holds and the recurring licence buys something real. Note what this does and does not settle: it shows the data model supports translated product data. It does not measure translation quality, and it does not test the free alternatives, so it justifies the line item without proving it is the cheapest way to satisfy FIX-04.
notes: FIX-04, NFR-04, SSC-12, SSC-21. WPML chosen 9 September 2026 as the translation plugin; no plugin is named in any client document, which says only 'translation plugin, about 107 USD a year', and R-14 has the client buying the licence in their own name. Tested against WPML 4.9.7 with WooCommerce Multilingual and String Translation. Method changed from playwright to wp-cli: the question is about the data layer, and a browser test would only observe the same rows through a template.

question: Does the native WordPress LIKE search fail to return relevant results for Arabic and Franco-Arabic search terms, as the Technical Design assumes?
expected: WordPress search is a LIKE query. It has no synonyms, no correction and no relevance. Section 7 row 9.
observed: WordPress 7.1, WooCommerce 11.1.0. Two products seeded: one named in Arabic, one Latin decoy named "Attar Bottle" that contains the Franco-Arabic string. Asking only whether each term reaches THE ARABIC product: exact Arabic name FOUND, first Arabic word alone FOUND, orthographic variant not found, Franco-Arabic "attar" not found. Native search is substring matching and nothing more. It reaches the Arabic product only when the query is literally contained in the name, and fails both the orthographic variant and the Franco-Arabic rendering. There is no relevance to tune, which is exactly why SRCH-06 and SRCH-07 specify a curated synonym and correction list rather than a scoring change. Note on the first run of this probe: searching "attar" does return a row, because the Latin decoy contains that string. Counting rows would report success where an Arabic shopper finds nothing.

question: Does the WooCommerce CSV importer correctly detect Arabic encoding, and does re-running an import safely update existing rows by SKU rather than duplicating them?
expected: Woo ships a basic CSV importer with fixed column handling, no dry run, no saved mappings, and no safe re run semantics. Section 7 row 6.
observed: WooCommerce 11.1.0 ships WC_Product_CSV_Importer with 33 methods. A dry-run method: no. A saved-mapping method: no. A UTF-8 CSV with a BOM and an Arabic product name was imported twice with update_existing on. Pass one imported 1 and updated 0; pass two imported 0 and updated 0. Products carrying SKU P008-SKU-1 afterwards: 1. The Arabic name round-tripped intact: yes. Encoding and re-run by SKU are both sound, but there is no dry run and no saved mapping, so section 7 row 6 is right that the native importer does not meet MIG-01 to MIG-25. The gap is the operator safety net, not the parsing.

question: Does WooCommerce's native stock validation and decrement hold under concurrent checkout, so that concurrent purchases of the last unit of stock result in one sale and not two?
expected: Section 6 classifies stock validation and decrement under concurrency as Native: reduce stock at payment, restore on cancel, which is BR-007.
observed: WooCommerce 11.1.0. wc_update_product_stock delegates to the data store: yes. The product data store issues arithmetic SQL for stock changes (meta_value +/- operand): yes. Two sequential decreases of 1 from a stock of 1 left the quantity at -1, so the write itself does not refuse to go negative. The guard against overselling is a validation step before payment (present), not the write. NOT TESTED: true simultaneity. One PHP process cannot place two checkouts at the same instant, so this probe cannot say whether two buyers of the last unit both succeed. What it establishes is the mechanism: an arithmetic SQL write is atomic per statement, but validation and decrement are separate steps, so a gap exists in principle. Settling BR-003 needs a parallel load test against a staging site, and that should be booked rather than assumed. Section 6 calls this Native. The write is atomic, which supports that, but the check-then-write gap is real and untested, so Native is not yet earned for the concurrent case.
notes: BR-003, CHK-12, AC-05. Section 6 row, not a section 7 gap row: the design claims this one is already solved. Verdict is partial because one PHP process cannot create simultaneity. The parallel load test that settles it is booked as MustafaShaaban/mizzey-platform#233, sprint 8, Stage 3, against #120 US-07-06. Update this row from partial when that test has run.

question: Does the CoreX header, mobile navigation, mega menu and footer system mirror correctly in right to left at every tested breakpoint?
expected: CoreX section 4 rates the header, mobile navigation, mega menu and footer system as Stable. The Technical Design and the acceptance criteria under FIX-04 and NFR-04 assume the storefront renders right to left with correct alignment, Arabic typography and spacing, mirrored directional icons, and no broken layout at any tested breakpoint.
notes: No single section 7 gap row names this; it tests the CoreX Stable claim against NAV-01 to NAV-10, SSC-07, SSC-08 and the RTL acceptance criteria in US-01-01. NOT RUN 9 September 2026: it needs a storefront with real navigation, a mega menu, a footer and Arabic content at several breakpoints. The runtime is a bare install with none of those, so a pass would prove nothing and a failure would only be measuring the absence of content. Blocked until the storefront exists.

question: Does WooCommerce's native free shipping method support only a minimum order amount or coupon condition, with no item count condition, as the Technical Design assumes?
expected: Free shipping supports a minimum order amount or a coupon. It has no item count condition. Section 7 row 2.
observed: WC_Shipping_Free_Shipping offers 5 condition(s):  = No requirement; coupon = A valid free shipping coupon; min_amount = A minimum order amount; either = A minimum order amount OR coupon; both = A minimum order amount AND coupon. Instance fields: title, requires, min_amount, ignore_discounts. No item count or quantity condition exists. The only threshold field is min_amount, an order total. BR-002 is custom work under either reading of OD-04, so the OD-04 answer changes the rule but not the fact that it must be written.

question: Does WooCommerce lack a Returned to Origin order status, and does an unrecognised carrier status currently risk being mapped to Delivered?
expected: Woo has no such status, and the carrier integration has reported cases of mapping a returned parcel to Delivered. Section 7 row 10.
observed: WooCommerce 11.1.0 ships 8 order statuses: wc-pending, wc-processing, wc-on-hold, wc-completed, wc-cancelled, wc-refunded, wc-failed, wc-checkout-draft. A returned-to-origin status: none. Bosta plugin 4.5.7 maps state codes to Woo statuses: 45 to completed, 46 to completed, 48 to cancelled, 100 to cancelled, 101 to cancelled, 104 to cancelled, 20 to processing, 999999 to processing. An unrecognised state falls back to 'processing', not completed, so the feared silent Delivered does not come from the fallback. The exposure is elsewhere: states 45 and 46 are grouped as "Finished successfully" and BOTH map to completed, while only 45 sets a delivery date. Two different terminal outcomes collapse into one Woo status. The plugin ships no legend for these codes anywhere in its source, so what 46 means cannot be established from the integration itself and must come from Bosta documentation or an account. That absence is exactly what SHIP-14 exists to fix. Driving the webhook handler with state 46 on an order that was processing left it processing, and wrote meta bosta_state_code='46', bosta_status='P-012 probe payload'. The mapping is DORMANT. In handle_status_update the call to map_bosta_state_to_wc_status is commented out, so the plugin never changes order status from a webhook: it only records meta. Nothing is silently marked Delivered today, so the expectation as written is refuted. Two consequences follow. SHIP-13, carrier status reflected on the order, is NOT delivered by this plugin as shipped, which bears on the partial leverage on US-09-04. And the dormant mapping is a trap: whoever enables it inherits 45 and 46 both becoming completed.
notes: ORD-13, SHIP-17, AC-16. Re-run 9 September 2026 against the real integration, Bosta WooCommerce 4.5.7, installed on the runtime. Refuted: the mapping is commented out in handle_status_update, so nothing is silently marked Delivered today, and an unknown state falls back to processing rather than completed. The exposure is that states 45 and 46 both map to completed while only 45 sets a delivery date, and the plugin ships no legend for the codes. What state 46 means is a blocking input from Bosta documentation, raised as mizzey-platform#234. Recorded on the board at mizzey-platform#166 (SHIP-14) and #165 (SHIP-13).

question: Does WooCommerce ship only the Shop Manager and Customer roles, with no built-in path to the six granular staff roles the contract requires?
expected: Woo ships Shop Manager and Customer only. Section 7 row 15.
observed: Roles on the site: administrator, editor, author, contributor, subscriber, customer, shop_manager. Beyond WordPress core, WooCommerce contributes: customer, shop_manager. shop_manager carries 93 capabilities. Report-related ones: view_woocommerce_reports. Report access is a single all-or-nothing capability, so hiding product cost or margin from one role while showing the rest of a report is not expressible in the capability model and is custom work. Shop Manager and Customer only. The six contracted staff roles and the reporting access matrix are entirely Mizzey work, as section 7 row 15 assumes.
notes: ROLE-03 to ROLE-09, ADM-130. Story trace records the range as 'ROLE-01 to ROLE-09'.

question: Does the native WooCommerce refund API enforce a ceiling at the amount actually paid to the gateway, for both full and partial refunds?
expected: Section 6 states the Woo refund API enforces the paid amount ceiling, which is BR-006, for full and partial refunds against the gateway.
observed: WooCommerce 11.1.0. Order 32 total 100.0. A 30 partial refund was accepted. A further refund of 200 against 70 remaining was REJECTED: Invalid refund amount. Total refunded now stands at 30.0 against a paid total of 100.0. The ceiling holds: partials are allowed and the total cannot exceed what was paid. BR-006 is native and section 6 is right that this one is already solved. Scope note: this tests the Woo bookkeeping ceiling only. Whether Paymob enforces the same limit on the gateway side is a separate question and is not tested here.
notes: PAY-07, PAY-08, PAY-17, ADM-91. Section 6 row, not a section 7 gap row: the design claims this one is already solved.

question: Does WooCommerce provide no wishlist functionality out of the box, and would a guest wishlist that is later built be exposed to the same replace-not-merge failure mode identified for the cart in row 1?
expected: Nothing. WooCommerce provides no wishlist functionality. Section 7 row 13.
observed: WooCommerce 11.1.0: wishlist functions found none; wishlist classes found none; wishlist tables found none. Guest state in Woo rides on WC_Session_Handler (present) backed by mz_woocommerce_sessions, and the persistent cart is user meta. A guest wishlist has no equivalent, so whatever carries it across login has to be written, and it is the same replace-versus-merge decision as row 1. Designing the two together is cheaper than discovering the second one after the first is built. Nothing wishlist-shaped exists in WooCommerce. WISH-01 to WISH-07 and ENT-07 are entirely custom, as section 7 row 13 assumes.

question: Does WooCommerce provide a native product cost field on products and variations, or must ADM-27 be a field Mizzey adds?
expected: US-16-05 is classified Native, and the Technical Design section 9 calls ADM-27 a New field on product and variation. Those two disagree. If Woo core carries no cost field, Native is wrong for this story and the classification, not the design, is the thing to correct.
observed: WooCommerce 11.1.0 ships a Cost of Goods Sold feature. WC_Product::get_cogs_value and set_cogs_value both exist. Feature enabled by default: no (option woocommerce_feature_cost_of_goods_sold_enabled = no). A cost of 137.5 set on a product survived save and reload (read back 137.5). The field is native but OFF by default, so it must be switched on deliberately as part of the build. `native` on US-16-05 is defensible; the Technical Design "New field" row is not, but the feature flag is a real build step. Feature flag restored to disabled after the test.
notes: ADM-27, RPT-11, OD-12. US-16-05 is key, so it is in the risk set. Check the installed Woo version for a cost of goods feature before concluding, and record the version in observed: a newer Woo may carry one that older guidance says it does not.

question: When an order is placed, is the product cost frozen onto the order line item the way the price is, or does the line read a mutable current cost?
expected: ENT-08 records the price snapshot as native but says nothing about cost. If cost is not frozen at the point of sale, editing a product cost silently rewrites every historical margin, and ADM-27's promise of accurate history does not hold. This is the one gap that cannot be repaired later, because the cost that applied on the day is gone.
observed: Cost of Goods Sold was off, enabled for the test and restored afterwards. Order 23 placed with 2 units at cost 100. Order cost at sale: 200.0. Product cost then changed to 999. Same order re-read from storage: 200.0. The order kept the cost that applied on the day. WooCommerce snapshots cost onto the order during calculate_totals, so ADM-27 accurate history holds without Mizzey adding anything, provided the feature is enabled before the first order.
notes: ADM-27, RPT-11, ENT-08, OD-12. Compare with P-002, which tests the price snapshot: price and cost are different promises and only one of them is in the register.

question: Does WooCommerce keep a structured, queryable record of when an order entered each status, or only prose in order notes?
expected: ADM-86 contracts an order timeline and US-18-02 classifies it native. SHIP-13 reflects carrier status onto the order. If transitions are queryable rows, dispatch and delivery times are derivable and ENT-10 needs no history. If the only per-transition record is an English sentence, a delivery-time or RTO-rate figure would have to parse prose, and the timestamps must be captured while the shipment table is being designed.
observed: WooCommerce 11.1.0. After pending to processing to on-hold to completed, the order carries: date_created=2026-09-09T09:49:27+00:00, date_modified=2026-09-09T09:49:29+00:00, date_paid=2026-09-09T09:49:29+00:00, date_completed=2026-09-09T09:49:29+00:00. No status-history table exists. Checked wc_order_status_history, wc_order_status_transitions, wc_order_history. 4 order note(s) recorded, of which 3 describe a status change. Example: "Order status changed from On hold to Completed." The only per-transition record is an English sentence in an order note, timestamped but not structured. date_paid and date_completed are the only queryable milestones, and neither is dispatch or delivery. A delivery-time or RTO-rate figure would have to parse note prose, which is not a foundation for a reported number. US-18-02 native is right for displaying a timeline and wrong for measuring one.
notes: ADM-86, SHIP-13, SHIP-16, SHIP-17, ENT-10. Asked because ENT-10 is contracted with a single status column and the client's C-RPT-15 wants average delivery time and RTO rate, which need transitions. Same shape as P-016: a story classified native on an assumption nobody tested.
